Female Bombay duck attain a maximum total length of 38.5 centimeters [Li = 38.5 centimeters], while males reach a somewhat smaller ultimate size of 37.7 centimeters [Li = 37.7 centimeters]. These values are derived from extensive field surveys conducted across the northern Arabian Sea and represent the upper bounds recorded for the species. The modest sexual dimorphism in size is consistent with observations in related lizardfish species, where females often achieve slightly greater lengths. Individuals hatch from pelagic eggs measuring approximately 0.9 millimeters in diameter, and the resulting yolk-sac larva emerges at an exceedingly minimal wet weight at birth of 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams], a mass that underscores the substantial energetic challenge facing the newly hatched larva as it transitions from endogenous yolk reserves to the onset of exogenous feeding on copepod nauplii. This tiny initial mass is characteristic of species producing numerous small, pelagic eggs.

Female Bombay duck undergo sexual maturation at a total length at puberty of 21.4 centimeters [Lp = 21.4 centimeters], a size threshold corresponding roughly to the end of the first year of life under optimal thermal conditions. Reaching this milestone marks the initiation of gonadal recrudescence and the capacity to participate in the species' protracted spawning season. Field data indicate that reproductive activity begins once females attain this length, which allows them to produce a substantial number of small, buoyant oocytes. The length-based metric for the onset of maturity is particularly useful for fisheries management, as it provides a readily measurable indicator of the proportion of the population that has entered the breeding stock. Males typically reach maturity at a slightly smaller size, though the precise length at puberty for males has not been as thoroughly documented in the literature for this species.

The maximum reproductive rate for Bombay duck has been estimated under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. At this temperature, individual females are capable of producing roughly 71,507 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = roughly 71,507 eggs per spawning event] and approximately 6 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 6 spawning events per year], a combination reflecting their high fecundity. This output is derived from an allometric relationship scaling with female body mass, whereby a gravid female of 233 grams at a total length of 33 centimeters produces tens of thousands of oocytes per spawning event. The species is an iteroparous, batch spawner, releasing multiple clutches over several months during the monsoon season, and the sustained production of such large numbers of eggs allows for rapid population turnover and recruitment into the pelagic larval pool.

Adult females ultimately attain an asymptotic wet weight of 233 grams [Wwi = 233 grams] at a total length of 33 centimeters, while adult males reach an ultimate wet weight of around 150 grams [Wwi = around 150 grams] at approximately 31 centimeters in length. These mass-at-length relationships were obtained from comprehensive morphometric sampling of commercial catches along the northwest coast of India. The pronounced difference in body mass between the sexes at comparable sizes is partially attributable to the greater reproductive investment of females, which carry large, hydrated ovaries during the spawning season. The weight-length relationship for the species follows a classic power-law curve, and these specific values serve as reference points for growth curve estimation and for calculating condition factor indices used to assess the overall health of local populations under varying fishing pressures.

The maximum lifespan of Bombay duck in the wild is approximately 1,095 days [am = approximately 1,095 days] at 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This relatively short longevity is typical of fast-growing, early-maturing, pelagic-spawning fish that experience high natural mortality. Tagging studies and otolith-based age validation have confirmed that very few individuals survive beyond their third year, with senescence and post-reproductive mortality occurring rapidly after the main spawning seasons. The constrained lifespan, when combined with the species' high fecundity, points toward a life-history strategy heavily skewed toward rapid growth and early, prolific reproduction. This strategy is well suited to the variable and productive coastal upwelling environments of the northern Indian Ocean, where the Bombay duck thrives as a dominant component of the demersal fish community.
